questions: Does wheel_radius 0.04 m with base_speed at its maximum raise the progress reached before the first off-track event, compared with iteration 1 (0.47 oval progress)?
Does the lower mass and shorter body (0.5 kg, 0.12 m) reduce steering_oscillation, or does it rise above the iteration-1 level of about 0.28?
Where does the first off-track event occur (track, bend, progress, and time)? Please use per-step telemetry if available.
Is the signal still smooth at the 12 mm footprint with 0.025 m spacing, or do readings jump at the outer sensors?
Which geometry or drivetrain limit now constrains the controller most: wheel_radius, mass, wheel_track or sensor spread?

intent: Return the sensor array to the best-measured iteration-1 layout (5 sensors, 0.025 m spacing, +/-0.05 m, 0.03 m lead, 12 mm footprint) and push the drivetrain further: larger wheels (0.04 m) for more ground speed, and lower mass (0.5 kg) with a shorter body (0.12 m) for less yaw inertia. Expected: oval progress above 0.5, max_error at or below 0.06 m, and fewer off-track endings than iteration 1.
learning: Across four iterations the sensor-array changes (7 sensors at 16 mm, 5 sensors at 8 mm) did not beat the 5-sensor 12 mm layout, while the drivetrain change in iteration 1 produced the only large gain. The next test therefore isolates drivetrain speed and yaw inertia on the best sensor layout. If progress rises but off-track endings persist, the next lever is the sensor lead (0.03 m vs 0.05 m) or a higher wheel_track to limit oscillation. If oscillation rises above 0.3 without a progress gain, the robot is overshooting and mass or wheel_track should move back toward iteration 1.
rationale:
Scores so far: iteration 0 = 52.3, iteration 1 = 114.4 (best), iteration 2 = 65.7, iteration 3 = 102.8. Every run in every iteration has ended off track, with 0 finishes. The limit is the off-track distance (max(0.06, 0.0125 + body_width/4)). Even at the maximum body_width of 0.18 m, that limit is 0.0575 m, so the 0.06 m floor governs and body width cannot buy tolerance. Max error sits at 0.061 to 0.066 m in every iteration while RMS error stays at 0.023 to 0.031 m. The robot tracks well until a single excursion takes it over the edge.

What the sensor tests showed: iteration 2 (7 sensors, 16 mm footprint) cut oval progress from 0.47 to 0.23, and iteration 3 (5 sensors, 8 mm footprint) gave 0.41 with slightly worse score than iteration 1. The 12 mm, 5-sensor array of iteration 1 is the best sensor configuration tested. Neither a larger nor a smaller footprint improved on it, so the sensor layout is close to its useful optimum and further sensor changes are unlikely to fix the excursions.

What the drivetrain change showed: the largest gain (52 to 114) came in iteration 1, when wheel_radius rose from 0.03 to 0.035, wheel_track narrowed to 0.10, mass fell to 0.6 kg and body_length fell to 0.14 m. Oval progress rose from 0.14 to 0.47. That points at speed and yaw response as the lever. Speed matters because the robot must cover the course in under 3 s, and with the current base speed it is still far from finishing. Lower yaw inertia (mass times length squared plus width squared, over 12) should let the robot correct faster after an excursion.

Decision: revert the sensor array to the iteration-1 layout (5 sensors at x = -0.05 to +0.05 with 0.025 m spacing, y = 0.03 m, 12 mm footprint), which is the best measured. Push the drivetrain further in the same direction: wheel_radius 0.035 to 0.04 m for more ground speed per PWM, mass 0.6 to 0.5 kg and body_length 0.14 to 0.12 m to cut yaw inertia further. I keep wheel_track at 0.10 m because it is already a good turn-authority setting and the minimum of 0.08 m would risk oscillation. Expected result: oval progress above 0.5, a lower or equal max_error, and a shorter time to reach the excursion point. Risk: the faster and lighter robot may oscillate more (steering_oscillation above 0.28), or the higher speed may push it off track sooner on tight bends.
